title: Names of the Eucharist (CCC 1328–1332)
hookLine: Lord's Supper, breaking of bread, holy sacrifice, Holy Communion, Holy Mass

cards: Evening, on the road to a village called Emmaus. Two disciples are walking out of Jerusalem, heartbroken, and a stranger falls in beside them. He explains the Scriptures to them all the way there.
They beg him to stay for supper. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them, and in that moment they recognize him, and he vanishes.
That same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell the others. Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it this way: "they knew him in the breaking of bread."
That phrase became one of the names for what Catholics celebrate at every Mass. Only one of them.

teach.b: This path walked that road on day sixty-nine; today, the names. The Catechism says this sacrament is so rich that no one name can hold it, and each name brings something out.

teach.h: THE SUPPER, THE BREAKING OF BREAD.
teach.b: Eucharist means thanksgiving, tied to the Greek words in the Last Supper accounts, where Jesus gives thanks, and to the Jewish blessings that praise God over bread and wine.
The Lord's Supper, because of the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before he died, and because it looks ahead to the wedding feast of the Lamb. The breaking of bread, the Emmaus name.

In Acts it's what the first Christians kept doing; the Douay-Rheims says they persevered "in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." The memorial of the Lord's Passion and Resurrection.
The Holy Sacrifice, because it makes present the one sacrifice of Christ. The Holy and Divine Liturgy, because the Church's whole liturgy finds its center here.
The Most Blessed Sacrament, the name for the Eucharist kept in the tabernacle. Holy Communion, because through it people are united to Christ, and to each other in one body. And last, Holy Mass.
The name comes from the end of the liturgy, the Catechism says, from the Latin word for sending, missio, because the people are sent out to do God's will in their daily lives.
So the familiar name comes from the last line, the dismissal. Each name opens a different window on one thing: thanks, a supper, bread broken, a memorial, a sacrifice, communion, a sending.

how: Catholics in the Latin rite usually say Mass for the celebration and Holy Communion for receiving; Eastern Catholics speak of the Divine Liturgy, and the reserved Eucharist is called the Blessed Sacrament.

games.q: what does “names of the eucharist” mean?
o: titles given to the priests who say Mass
thanksgiving, supper, breaking of bread, Mass
the saints whose names are said at the altar

games.q: the names and what they show — tap the pairs.
p: how the Emmaus disciples knew him
united to Christ and one another
from the sending at the end

s: the name Mass comes from the sending at the end
the Catechism links it to the Latin missio: the people are sent out to do God's will.
breaking of bread is a modern nickname
Luke uses it at Emmaus, and Acts says the first Christians persevered in it.
each name of the Eucharist is a different rite
they're many names for one gift, each bringing out something different.

games.q: you're one of the two on the road to Emmaus. the stranger has explained the Scriptures all the way. at the table, when do you recognize him?
o: when he tells you his name.
when he takes, blesses, breaks and gives the bread.
only the next day, in Jerusalem.
games.why: "they knew him in the breaking of bread." then he vanished, and that same hour they went back to Jerusalem.

practice: On each out-breath, say one name, quietly or in your mind: Eucharist, the Lord's Supper, the breaking of bread, the memorial, the Holy Sacrifice, the Divine Liturgy, the Blessed Sacrament, Holy Communion, Holy Mass.
Then go back to whichever name caught you and stay with it, asking what it shows that the others don't. If you pray, rest there in thanks.

wordCard.voice: Names of the Eucharist. Thanksgiving, supper, breaking of bread, memorial, sacrifice, liturgy, sacrament, communion, Mass: many names, each opening a window on one gift. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: thanksgiving; the Catechism ties the name to the giving of thanks at the Last Supper.

carryVoice: Your line: one gift, many names. Even the everyday name is a sending. That's today, done.
